Indicators: Is the country party to the UN Convention on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women?

Indicators: Does the Constitution enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Analysis [EN]: The de facto authorities have not adopted a Constitution yet.

Indicators: Does the legislation enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Analysis [EN]: Since September 2021, girls are banned from secondary education by the de facto authorities, as well as from post-secondary education since the 20th December 2022.---See: https://www.unesco.org/en/education/emergencies/afghanistan for secondary education and https://twitter.com/hrw/status/1605255842420367370/photo/1 for higher education

Indicators: Are 9 years of primary and secondary education legally compulsory?

Indicators: Are 12 years of primary and secondary education legally free?
Analysis [EN]: The applicable legal framework is unclear. The Education law of 2008 used to provide for at least 12 years of secondary education. ---See: https://www.unesco.org/en/education/emergencies/afghanistan for secondary education and https://twitter.com/hrw/status/1605255842420367370/photo/1 for higher education

Indicators: Is pre-primary education legally free and compulsory?
Analysis [EN]: The applicable legal framework is unclear. The Education law of 2008 used to provide for free pre-school education but there was no reference to compulsory pre-school education.

Indicators: Is equal access to post-secondary education legally guaranteed?
Analysis [EN]: Since the 20th December 2022 girls are de facto banned from post-secondary education.---See:  https://twitter.com/hrw/status/1605255842420367370/photo/1

Indicators: Is the legal age of marriage set at least at 18 years old?
Analysis [EN]: In December 2021, the de facto authorities have issued a decree on women’s rights, which says that they should not get married without their own consent, but that decree does not specify a minimum age of marriage.

Indicators: Is the minimum age of employment at least 15 and aligned with the end of compulsory education?
Analysis [EN]: The applicable legal framework is unclear. Girls are banned from education after the 6th grade. Their right to work is also limited with several bans applying to various fields of work.--- See: UN Women: Women’s rights in Afghanistan one year after the Taliban take-over. (2022).

Indicators: Are learners legally protected against all violence and corporal punishment in educational institutions?
Analysis [EN]: The applicable legal framework is unclear. The 2008 Education Law used to prohibit corporal punishment in schools.

Indicators: Is pregnant and parenting girls’ right to education protected in the legal framework?
Analysis [EN]: While there is no information specifically related to legal provision on pregnant and parenting girls, since September 2021, girls are de facto banned from secondary education by the de facto authorities, as well as from post-secondary education since the 20th December 2022.

Indicators: General comments
Analysis [EN]: The Taliban's government (de facto authority) has not been recognized by the international community. The applicable legal framework is unclear. This profile outlines the regulations enforced by the de facto authorities since August 2021. While some of these rules are not fully formalized in written form or legal documents, they are included here as they are implemented at the national level.

Indicators: Does the Constitution enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Result: Yes, without discrimination based on sex/gender
Analysis [EN]: The Constitution of Afghanistan enshrines the right to education but it is limited to citizens and therefore does not apply to all within the territory. It contains a general principle of non-discrimination which do not mention the ground of sex, and an equality principle between men and women.Constitution of Afghanistan of 2004 Article 22. Any kind of discrimination and distinction between citizens of Afghanistan shall be forbidden. The citizens of Afghanistan, man and woman, have equal rights and duties before the law.Article 43. Education is the right of all citizens of Afghanistan …

Indicators: Does the legislation enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Analysis [EN]: The Education Law of 1387 (2008) enshrines the right to education without discrimination but does not expressly mention the ground of sex. Furthermore, the right to education is limited to citizens and does not apply to all within the territory.Education Law of 1387 (2008) Article 3. The citizens of the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan have equal rights to education without any kind of discrimination.

Indicators: Are 9 years of primary and secondary education legally compulsory?
Analysis [EN]: The Education Law of 1387 (2008) specifies that intermediate education is compulsory from first to ninth grade but there is lack of clarity of the age of completion in article 5(1) in light of article 17. Intermediate education in Afghanistan is composed of nine grades.Education Law of 1387 (2008) Article 4(1). The intermediate (basic) education in Afghanistan is compulsory.Article 5(1). Children, from age six to the completion of age nine, are compulsory enrolled in the intermediate (basic) education schools level.Article 17. Intermediate (Basic) educational level comprises grade first to the end of grade ninth, provided free and compulsory in a balanced and equitable manner.

Indicators: Are 12 years of primary and secondary education legally free?
Analysis [EN]: Free education for at least 12 years is enshrined both in the Constitution of Afghanistan of 2004 and the Education Law of 1387 (2008).Constitution of Afghanistan of 2004 Article 43. Education … shall be offered up to the B.A. level in the state educational institutes free of charge by the state.Education Law of 1387 (2008) Article 4(2). Pre- school educational level , intermediate (basic) education, secondary, technical professional, vocational, artistic, formal Islamic education, higher education, (Thirteenth and fourteenth grades) teachers’ training , literacy and basic practical education in the public educational and training institutions are provided for free.

Indicators: Is pre-primary education legally free and compulsory?
Analysis [EN]: The Education Law of 1387 (2008) specifies that pre-school education is provided for free but it does not state that it is compulsory and the duration is not specified.Education Law of 1387 (2008)Article 4(2). Pre- school educational level … are provided for free.Article 5(2). Children, whose ages are over kindergarten and lower than the school enrollment age, shall be enrolled in the pre-school education level.

Indicators: Is equal access to post-secondary education legally guaranteed?
Analysis [EN]: No legal provision has been identified concerning equal access to post-secondary education. The Education Law of 1387 (2008) contains a provision on TVET but only states that it is provided and expanded in public educational institutions in an equitable manner.Education Law of 1387 (2008) Article 23(1). Technical-professional, vocational and artistic education level comprises grade tenth to the end of grade fourteenth, provided and expanded in public educational institutions in a balanced and equitable manner, considering the number of population and Kochis residing in the area and educational and training standards for the graduates of the intermediate (basic) educational schools.

Indicators: Is the legal age of marriage set at least at 18 years old?
Analysis [EN]: The Civil Code 1977 states that girls can marry at 16 years old with exceptions allowing for marriage at 15 years old.Civil Code of Afghanistan Article 70. Capacity to marry shall be complete when males attain 18 and females 16 years.Article 71(1). Marriage contract of a girl who has not attained the age mentioned in article (70) of this Law may only be concluded by her competent father or competent court. (2). Marriage contract of minor girls under 15 years old are not permissible by no means.

Indicators: Is the minimum age of employment at least 15 and aligned with the end of compulsory education?
Analysis [EN]: In Afghanistan, compulsory education starts at age 6 for a minimum of nine years but the minimum age of employment is 14. Therefore, the minimum age of employment is below 15 and is not aligned with the end of compulsory education.Labour Law No 35 of 2007 Article 127. The young employee is the person who has completed 14 years of age but has not attained 18 years of age

Indicators: Are learners legally protected against all violence and corporal punishment in educational institutions?
Analysis [EN]: The Education Law of 1387 (2008) prohibits corporal punishment in schools. No legal provision that expressively prohibit gender-based violence in the education system has been identified.Education Law of 1387 (2008) Article 39. Every kind of physical and psychological punishment of students is prohibited even for their correction and chastisement. Violators shall be prosecuted in accordance with the legal provisions.

Indicators: Is pregnant and parenting girls’ right to education protected in the legal framework?
Analysis [EN]: No legal provision that prohibits restrictions to the right to education of pregnant and parenting girls has been identified.

Indicators: Does the Constitution enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Analysis [EN]: The Constitution of Belize does not comprehensively enshrine the right to education as it requires to protect the right to basic education only.It contains a provision on equality of rights and on non-discrimination on the ground of sex.Constitution of Belize of 1981, as amended in 2021 Whereas the people of Belize- (e) require policies of state ... which eliminate economic and social privilege and disparity among the citizens of Belize whether by race, ethnicity, colour, creed, disability or sex; which ensures gender equality; which protect the rights of the individual to life, liberty, basic education ...Article 6(1): All persons are equal before the law and are entitled without any discrimination to the equal protection of the law.Article 16:(1) ... no law shall make any provision that is discriminatory either of itself or in its effect.(2) ... no person shall be treated in a discriminatory manner by any person or authority.(3) In this section, the expression “discriminatory” means affording different treatment to different persons attributable wholly or mainly to their respective descriptions by sex, race, place of origin, political opinions, colour or creed whereby persons of one such description are subjected to disabilities or restrictions to which persons of another such description are not made subject or are accorded privileges or advantages which are not accorded to persons of another such description.

Indicators: Does the legislation enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Result: No, the right to education is not enshrined
Analysis [EN]: No disposition enshrining the right to education has been identified in the legislation. The Education and Training Act prohibits discrimination but only regarding the admission process in schools.Education and Training Act of 2010, as amended in 2024 Article 48: (1) No person shall be refused admission to any school on account of religion, race, ethnicity, language or political affiliation. (2) No person shall be refused admission to any school on account of sex, except where such schools are historically non-coeducational.Article 49: (1) The Ministry shall ensure equitable access for both sexes to education at all levels, and that provision of education is sensitive to the particular needs of both males and females, and caters to the special needs of challenged pupils.

Indicators: Are 9 years of primary and secondary education legally compulsory?
Analysis [EN]: The Education and Training Act of Belize guarantees compulsory primary and secondary education for a duration of ten years, from the age of five to 16 years old.  Education and Training Act of 2010, as amended in 2024 Article 2: … “child of compulsory school age” “means a child who is not less than 5 years of age but not more than sixteen years of age; Article 59: Every person having control of a child, who is five years old by the first day of September and who has not exceeded the age of sixteen, shall cause the child to regularly and annually attend some public or nonpublic school for the entire term … Education Rules of 2000, n. 92 Article 10: (3) Schools shall be and are hereby categorized based on the level and/or type of education offered. Current categories of schools in the formal system of education are: (b) Primary Schools: are schools providing basic education normally organized as eight years of schooling; (c) Secondary Schools: are schools providing general secondary education normally organised as four years of schooling and whose matriculation requirements include the completion of primary education; Article 111:  (2) The ages for attendance of students at primary schools shall be between five years and fourteen years, provided that a Principal may admit a child who will have reached the age of five years by the end of January of the school year of admission and may retain a child who is older than fourteen years at his discretion. (3) Students shall be admitted to secondary schools after completion of primary education.

Indicators: Are 12 years of primary and secondary education legally free?
Analysis [EN]: If citizens and residents should have access to education without tuition fees, special fees might be put in place, therefore free education is not guaranteed.Education and Training Act of 2010, as amended in 2024 Article 70. (1) Citizens and permanent residents are entitled, as of right to be admitted to any government and government-aided primary school without payment of tuition fees. Special fees may be levied with the approval of the Chief Education Officer(2) Citizens and permanent residents of Belize are entitled, as of right, to be admitted to any government secondary school without payment of tuition fees. Special fees may be levied with the approval of the Chief Education Officer.Education Rules of 2000, n. 92 Article 142: (5) Parents or guardians are expected to pay such school fees and make required contributions as are approved by the Ministry of Education in accordance with Rule 146 of these Rules.Article 146: (1) A Managing Authority of a Ministry of Education and government-aided school may charge fees, subject to the approval of the Chief Education Officer or the Minister, as is required by the Act. In approving such fees, the Chief Education Officer or Minister shall consult with the District Education Council and the National Council for Education, respectively.(4) No Ministry of Education or government-aided primary schools shall prohibit attendance at school of a child of compulsory school age because of the ability of the parent(s) or guardian(s) to pay school fees and such children shall not be subject to discrimination by the school.

Analysis [EN]: The Constitution of Benin does not enshrine the right to education but it does guarantee the education of children. Indicators: Does the legislation enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Analysis [EN]: The law on the Children's Code provides that the right to education is guaranteed, but this applies only to children. There is a principle of non-discrimination.Law No. 2015-08 of 8 December 2015 on the Childrens Code in the Republic of Benin (unofficial translation)Article 112. The State guarantees the right of the child to education ... Parents have the obligation to enrol their children in school without any form of discrimination.

Indicators: Are 9 years of primary and secondary education legally compulsory?
Analysis [EN]: While the Law of 2012 on the prevention and punishment of violence against women stipulates that schooling is compulsory until the age of 16 years, the Constitution and the Law on national education policy only guarantee six years of compulsory primary education.The Constitution of Benin of 1990 (non-official translation) Article 13. ... Primary education is compulsory ...Law No. 2003-17 of 11 November 2003 on the national education policy in the Republic of Benin, amended in 2005 (non-official translation) Article 24. Primary education is compulsory ... It has a normal duration of six years ... This level of education includes children aged four and a half years and over.Law No. 2011-26 of 9 January 2012 on the prevention and punishment of violence against women (unofficial translation)Article 4. School attendance is compulsory for all children up to the age of 16 years, regardless of sex, race or religion.

Indicators: Are 12 years of primary and secondary education legally free?

Primary education is compulsory. The State shall gradually introduce free schooling in State educational institutions, in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution ...

Indicators: Is pre-primary education legally free and compulsory?
Analysis [EN]: The law provides that preschool education, for a period of two years, is provided free of charge, but no provision concerning the compulsory nature of this level of education has been identified.Law No. 2003-17 of 11 November 2003 on the national education policy in the Republic of Benin, amended in 2005 (non-official translation) Article 23. Indicators: Is the legal age of marriage set at least at 18 years old?
Analysis [EN]: The law on the Childrens Code in the Republic of Benin prohibits the marriage of persons under 18 years of age, except for exemptions granted under the Family Code. However, while the Childrens Code stipulates that the legal age for marriage is 18 years, marriage is also possible for a minor with the consent of the person holding parental authority, without a minimum age requirement being defined. A judicial exception is also provided for, without defining a minimum age requirement.Law No. 2015-08 of 8 December 2015 on the Childrens Code in the Republic of Benin (unofficial translation)Article 375. Any person who gives in marriage a child under the age of 18 years, except for exemptions granted under the Family Code, shall be punished by imprisonment ...Law No. 2002-07 of 24 August 2004 on the Family Code (non-official translation) Article 120. Minors under the age of 18 years may not enter into marriage without the consent of the person holding parental authority ...Article 123. Marriage may only be entered into between a man of at least 18 years of age and a woman of at least 18 years of age, unless a waiver from the age requirement is granted on serious grounds by order of the President of the Court of First Instance at the request of the Public Prosecutors Office.

Indicators: Is the minimum age of employment at least 15 and aligned with the end of compulsory education?
Analysis [EN]: The minimum age for employment (14 years) is under 15 years. Whether only primary education is compulsory or education is compulsory up to 16 years, there is no age alignment.Labour Code, Law No. 98-004 of 27 January 1998 Article 166. Children may not be employed in any enterprise before the age of 14 years.

Indicators: Are learners legally protected against all violence and corporal punishment in educational institutions?
Analysis [EN]: Several laws prohibit violence against women in schools. The law on the Childrens Code prohibits corporal punishment in schools.Law 2006-19 of 5 September 2006 on the punishment of sexual harassment and protection of victims in the Republic of Benin (non-official translation) Article 2. All forms of sexual harassment constitute an offence in the Republic of Benin, regardless of the status of the perpetrator or victim and regardless of where the act was committed.Article 6. No student may be punished or expelled for having suffered or refused to suffer sexual harassment by his or her educator or any other authority in his or her school.Article 7. No student may be punished or expelled for having testified to or reported the acts defined in Article 1.Law No. 2011-26 of 9 January 2012 on the prevention and punishment of violence against women (non-official translation) Article 2. Violence against women is defined … as any act of gender-based violence that results in, or is likely to result in, physical, sexual or psychological harm or suffering to women, including threats of such acts, coercion or arbitrary deprivation of liberty … The violations concern: … physical or moral violence, sexual and psychological violence committed within the community, including rape, sexual assault and abuse, sexual harassment as provided for by Law 2006-19 … and intimidation at work, in educational institutions and elsewhere, pimping, trafficking and forced prostitution.Law No. 2015-08 of 8 December 2015 on the Childrens Code in the Republic of Benin (unofficial translation)Article 119. Indicators: Is pregnant and parenting girls’ right to education protected in the legal framework?
Analysis [EN]: The law on the Childrens Code contains a provision concerning the continuation of education for pregnant girls and young mothers, but puts the obligation of the continuation of the young mothers’ education on the male responsible for the pregnancy, which cannot be considered as sufficiently protecting the right to education.Law No. 2015-08 of 8 December 2015 on the Childrens Code in the Republic of Benin (unofficial translation)Article 180. It is prohibited to impregnate minor. Any person who impregnates a female child, in spite of the provisions of this Law, is solely responsible for the consequences. Thus, any male responsible for the pregnancy of an adolescent has the obligation to ... ensure that the girl continues her studies or begins vocational training ...

Analysis [EN]: The Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina enshrines the right to education for all within its territory without discrimination based on sex.Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 1995 [1]Article II: Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ...3. Enumeration of RightsAll persons within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall enjoy the human rights and fundamental freedoms referred to in paragraph 2 above; these include: ... l) The right to education.4. Non-DiscriminationThe enjoyment of the rights and freedoms provided for in this Article or in the international agreements listed in Annex I to this Constitution shall be secured to all persons in Bosnia and Herzegovina without discrimination on any ground such as sex, race, color, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, birth or other status.[1] The Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the highest legal and political document of the State which defines Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state consisting of two entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Republika Srpska, and of the Brcko District as a separate administrative unit under the State sovereignty. The entity of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina constitutes of ten cantons. National Report submitted for the ninth consultation on the implementation of the Convention and Recommendation against Discrimination in Education (2012-2016), 2012, p. 3.

Indicators: Does the legislation enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Analysis [EN]: The Framework Law on Primary and Secondary Education provides a right of access and equal opportunities for participation in education but only to children. This right is to be ensured without discrimination on any basis, though gender and sex are not explicitly named as prohibited grounds.Framework Law on Primary and Secondary Education (2003)Article 4. Any child shall have equal right of access and equal opportunities for participation in appropriate education, without discrimination on any basis.Equal access and equal opportunities include ensuring of equal conditions and opportunities for all, for the beginning and continuation of further education.Article 23. Parents shall have the right and obligation to ensure education of their children.

Indicators: Are 9 years of primary and secondary education legally compulsory?
Analysis [EN]: Education is compulsory in Bosnia and Herzegovina from the age of six for a period of nine years, and although the law specifies mandatory ‘primary’ education only, the ISCED classification of this period of education translates to primary and lower secondary education.Framework Law on Primary and Secondary Education (2003) Article 16. Primary education shall be mandatory for all children. Mandatory education shall begin in the calendar year in which by April 1 the child shall have completed six years of life and shall last, without cessation, throughout the period that may not be shorter than eight years. The competent education authorities and schools in Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be obligated to create, no later than by June 2004, all the conditions required for normal start of primary school education in the duration of nine years.

Indicators: Are 12 years of primary and secondary education legally free?
Analysis [EN]: Education is free in Bosnia and Herzegovina from the age of six for a period of at least nine years, and thereafter secondary education is also free of charge. The Framework Law on Higher Education indicates that secondary education lasts for a duration of four years, though this is not clear from the Framework Law on Primary and Secondary Education.Framework Law on Primary and Secondary Education (2003)Article 16. Primary education shall be mandatory for all children. Mandatory education shall begin in the calendar year in which by April 1 the child shall have completed six years of life and shall last, without cessation, throughout the period that may not be shorter than eight years.The competent education authorities and schools in Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be obligated to create, no later than by June 2004, all the conditions required for normal start of primary school education in the duration of nine years.Mandatory education shall be free of charge. Primary education shall be ensured free of charge for all children. The child in terms of this Law shall include any person up to the completed eighteenth year of life.Article 17. … Secondary education at public institutions shall be free of charge, pursuant to the lawFramework Law on Higher Education in BiH (2007) Article 7. Access to higher education shall be available to all those who have completed the four-year secondary education in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Analysis [EN]: Corporal punishment is prohibited in schools. For the purpose of this Law, the following definitions shall apply: a) gender based violence: any act causing physical, mental, sexual or economic damage or suffering, as well as threats of such actions, which interfere with the enjoyment of rights and freedoms based on gender equality, in public and private life, including trafficking in human beings for the purpose of forced labor, and any restriction or arbitrary deprivation of liberty, for persons exposed to such acts;Article 17. All forms of gender based violence in private and public life is prohibited. Competent authorities shall undertake all appropriate measures in order to eliminate and prevent gender based violence in public and private life, and shall provide instruments of protection, assistance and compensation to the victims. Competent authorities shall also develop measures of protection of gender based violence, especially in education, in order to eliminate bias, customs and all other practices based on the idea of inferiority or superiority of either sex, as well as stereotype roles of men and women. Indicators: General comments
Analysis [EN]: Bosnia and Herzegovina is a State which consists of two entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska. The Brcko District is a separate administrative unit under the State sovereignty. The entity of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina constitutes of ten cantons. Although each of these twelve administrative units has its own Ministry of Education and education legislation, the Federal Ministry of Education and Science at the level of the Federation of BiH has a coordinating role over the cantonal ministries of education. To coordinate this system, four framework laws were adopted at state level, and all laws in the Republika Srpska, the ten cantons and the Brcko District are required to be harmonized with the provisions of these framework laws. For the purposes of this Atlas, UNESCO has limited its research on education legislation to those framework laws which therefore govern the entire territory.[1] [1] Education for All 2015 National Review Report:Bosnia and Herzegovina

Indicators: Does the Constitution enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Result: Yes, without discrimination based on sex/gender
Analysis [EN]: The Constitution of Bulgaria enshrines the right to education for all. There is a non-discrimination principle that explicitly mention the ground of sex. Constitution of the Republic of Bulgaria of 1991, as last amended in 2007Article 6. (1). All persons are born free and equal in dignity and rights. (2). All citizens shall be equal before the law. There shall be no privileges or restriction of rights on the grounds of race, national or social origin, ethnic self-identity, sex, religion, education, opinion, political affiliation, personal or social status or property status.Article 53(1). Everyone shall have the right to education.

Indicators: Does the legislation enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Analysis [EN]: The legislation enshrines the right to education and contains a general principle of non-discrimination but does not explicitly mention sex or gender as a prohibited ground for distinction. Pre-school and School Education Act Article 3 (2) Education is a national priority based on the following principles: 3. equal access to high-quality education and inclusion of every child and every pupil;  4. equal treatment and non-discrimination in pre-school and school education; Article 7 (1). Everybody shall have the right to education and may improve his or her education and qualifications through lifelong learning.  (2). The inclusive education shall constitute an integral part of the right to education.

Indicators: Are 9 years of primary and secondary education legally compulsory?
Analysis [EN]: Education from the age of seven to the age of sixteen is compulsory, for a period of nine years, covering primary and lower secondary education. Pre-school and School Education Act  Article 8 (2). School education shall be compulsory until the age of 16, starting from the school year which begins in the year in which the child becomes seven years of age. Article 38 (1). Depending on the stage or degree of education, non-specialized schools shall be:  1. elementary (grades I to IV inclusive);  2. primary (grades I to VII inclusive);  3. gymnasiums (grades VIII to XII inclusive);  4. integrated (grades I to X inclusive);  5. secondary (grades I to XII inclusive)

Indicators: Are 12 years of primary and secondary education legally free?
Analysis [EN]: Free primary and secondary education is guaranteed in municipal schools in Bulgaria for twelve years, starting the year the child turns seven. Pre-school and School Education Act  Article 9 (1). The compulsory pre-school and school education at state-owned and municipal kindergartens and schools shall be free for children and pupils. (4) The right to free education shall be exercised by not paying tuition fees for the training financed from the state budget, and using free-of-charge the facilities for training and development of the interests and abilities of children and pupils. No fees shall be paid also in the case of sitting for state matriculation exams and state exams for awarding professional qualifications in the theory and practice of the occupation for the purposes of acquiring a secondary education degree. Article 38 (1). Depending on the stage or degree of education, non-specialized schools shall be:  1. elementary (grades I to IV inclusive);  2. primary (grades I to VII inclusive);  3. gymnasiums (grades VIII to XII inclusive);  4. integrated (grades I to X inclusive);  5. secondary (grades I to XII inclusive)  …  (4) Non-specialized schools shall be municipal, except for vocational gymnasiums which shall be owned by the State.

Everyone living in Burkina Faso has the right to education without discrimination of any kind, including on the basis of sex, social origin, race, religion, political opinion, nationality or state of health. This right is exercised on the basis of equity and equal opportunities for all citizens.

Analysis [EN]: The Law on Education enshrines the right to education but no non-discrimination principle has been identified. Law on Education of 2007 Article 31. Every citizen has the right to access qualitative education of at least 9 years in public schools free of charge. The Ministry in charge of education shall gradually prepare the policy and strategic plans to ensure that all citizens obtain qualitative education as stipulated by this law.

Indicators: Are 9 years of primary and secondary education legally compulsory?
Analysis [EN]: The Constitution implies that education is compulsory for nine years however this is not explicit. Furthermore, the Law on Education does not provide for compulsory education.Constitution of Cambodia of 1993 as amended through to 2008 Article 68. The State shall provide free primary and secondary education to all citizens in public schools. Citizens shall receive education for at least 9 years. The State shall help promote and develop Pali schools and Buddhist institutes.Law on Education of 2007 Article 32. Enrolment of the children for grade 1 (one) of the formal general education program shall be set at an age of 6 (six) years or at least 70 (seventy) months on the date of the beginning of the school year.

Indicators: Are 12 years of primary and secondary education legally free?

The State shall help promote and develop Pali schools and Buddhist institutesLaw on Education of 2007 Article 31. Indicators: Is pre-primary education legally free and compulsory?
Analysis [EN]: No legal provision has been identified that provides for free or compulsory pre-primary education.Law on Education of 2007 Article 16. Indicators: Is equal access to post-secondary education legally guaranteed?
Analysis [EN]: No legal provision has been identified guaranteeing equal access to post-secondary education.

Indicators: Is the legal age of marriage set at least at 18 years old?
Analysis [EN]: The minimum age of marriage is 18 years but can be lowered to the age of 16 years with parental consent or consent of the guardian.Civil Code of 2007 Article 948. (Marriageable age) Neither men nor women may marry until they have reached the age of 18. However, if one of the parties has attained the age of majority and the other party is a minor at least 16 years of age, the parties may marry with the consent of the parental power holders or guardian of the minor.

Indicators: Is the minimum age of employment at least 15 and aligned with the end of compulsory education?
Analysis [EN]: The minimum working age is 15 years but the end of compulsory education is not explicitly defined.Labour Code of 1997 Article 177. 1. The allowable minimum age for wage employment is set at fifteen years 2. The minimum allowable age for any kind of employment or work, which, by its nature, could be hazardous to the health, the safety, or the morality of an adolescent, is eighteen years. The types of employment or work covered by this paragraph are determined by a Prakas (ministerial order) of the Ministry in Charge of Labor, in consultation with the Labor Advisory Committee ... 4. Regardless of the provisions of paragraph 1 above, children from twelve to fifteen years of age can be hired to do light work provided that: a) The work is not hazardous to their health or mental and physical development. b) The work will not affect their regular school attendance, their participation in guidance programs or vocational training approved by a competent authority.

Indicators: Are learners legally protected against all violence and corporal punishment in educational institutions?
Analysis [EN]: The Law on Education prohibits physical and mental punishment and a directive from the Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport, No. 922 MoEYS to the Director of Provincial Education, Youth and Sport on the subject of “Punishment for students” states “physical punishments such as hitting, kneeling down, standing under the sun”, as well as mental punishments such as imposing copying of lessons that is impossible to achieve and making students feel bad and humiliated and punishments such as forcing students to do inappropriate tasks, are banned in all educational institutions throughout the country.”[1]Law on Education of 2007 Article 35. The learners rights concerning education are: … The right to be respected and paid attention on human rights, especially the right to dignity, the right to be free from any form of torture or from physical and mental punishment.[1] End All Corporal Punishment, Corporal punishment of children in Cambodia, May 2019, http://www.endcorporalpunishment.org/wp-content/uploads/country-reports/Cambodia.pdf [accessed on 06/05/19]

Indicators: Is pre-primary education legally free and compulsory?
Analysis [EN]: No provision guaranteeing compulsory and free pre-primary education has been identified.

Indicators: Is equal access to post-secondary education legally guaranteed?
Analysis [EN]: The law on higher education policy guarantees equal access to this level of education.Law No. 005 of 16 April 2001 on higher education policy (non-official translation) Article 11 (1). In this regard: (a) the State shall protect any higher education applicant from discrimination on the grounds of race, gender, age, religion and linguistic or geographical origin; (b) the State shall encourage academic institutions to take appropriate measures or initiatives, in particular to facilitate access to higher education for persons with disabilities.

Indicators: Is the legal age of marriage set at least at 18 years old?
Analysis [EN]: The Cameroonian Penal Code punishes the marriage of children under 18 years of age. Forced marriage(3). Any person who gives in marriage a girl or boy under the age of (18) years shall be punished by the penalties provided for in paragraphs 1 and 2 above.Order No. 81/002 of 29 June 1951 on the organization of civil status and various provisions relating to the status of individuals (non-official translation) Article 52. No marriage may be celebrated: (1) if the girl is under 15 years of age or the boy under 18 years of age, unless exempted by the President of the Republic for serious reasons.

Indicators: Is the minimum age of employment at least 15 and aligned with the end of compulsory education?
Analysis [EN]: The minimum age for work is under 15 years and no legislative provision concerning the age at which compulsory schooling ends has been identified, which does not allow UNESCO to assess age alignment.Law No. 92-007 of 14 August 1992 on the Labour Code (non-official translation) Article 86. (1) Children may not be employed in any enterprise, even as apprentices, before the age of 14 years, unless an exemption is granted by order of the Minister of Labour, taking into account local circumstances and the tasks that may be required of them.

Indicators: Are learners legally protected against all violence and corporal punishment in educational institutions?
Analysis [EN]: The law on education policy in Cameroon prohibits all forms of violence in the education system. The physical and moral integrity of students is guaranteed in the education system. This means that physical abuse and all other forms of violence, discrimination of any kind, as well as the sale, distribution and consumption of alcoholic beverages, tobacco and drugs are prohibited.[1] Committee on the Rights of the Child, Concluding observations on the combined third to fifth periodic reports of Cameroon, 6 July 2017, para 24 https://tbinternet.ohchr.org/_layouts/15/treatybodyexternal/Download.aspx?symbolno=CRC%2fC%2fCMR%2fCO%2f3-5&Lang=en [Accessed on 25 April 2019]

Indicators: Is pregnant and parenting girls’ right to education protected in the legal framework?
Analysis [EN]: It has been reported that Circular No. 02/22/C/MINESEC/CAB adopted in [1] provides for pregnant students to remain in school until the 26th week of pregnancy and for re-entry conditions for young mothers [2]. UNESCO was not able to consult this circular directly. The adoption of this circular puts an end to the previous ban on pregnant girls attending school. ---[1] Ministry of Secondary Education, Pregnancy and School Exams: Births in the 2022 Session (accessed 27/09/2022)[2] Human Rights Watch, A brighter future: Empowering Pregnant Girls and Mothers to Stay in School

Indicators: Does the Constitution enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Result: No, the right to education is not enshrined
Analysis [EN]: Canada has no written constitution in one single document, but a number of Constitution Acts. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms does not enshrine the right to education, although contains provisions on the right to minority language education. There is a provision on equality and non-discrimination which contains sex as a prohibited ground.Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (First Part of the Constitutional Act of 1982)Article 15. (1) Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.(2) Subsection (1) does not preclude any law, program or activity that has as its object the amelioration of conditions of disadvantaged individuals or groups including those that are disadvantaged because of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.Article 28. Notwithstanding anything in this Charter, the rights and freedoms referred to in it are guaranteed equally to male and female persons.

Analysis [EN]: The legal age of marriage is 18 years old for both women and men, however, marriage is permitted for girls aged 14 years and for boys aged 16 years with the consent of the parents, grandparents, legal guardian or the court. The Constitution adopted in 2019 gives two years to the National Assembly to start the consultation process popular and referendum on the draft Code Family.Constitution of the Republic of Cuba of 2019 (unofficial translation) Title XI …Transitory dispositions Eleven: Based on the results of the Popular Consultation held, the National Assembly of Peoples Power will have, within two years of validity of the Constitution, start the consultation process popular vote and referendum on the draft Family Code, which should include the way to establish marriage.Family Code (Law No. 1289) of 1975Article 3. The female and male over 18 years of age are authorized to formalize the marriage. Consequently, minors under the age of 18 are not allowed to enter into marriage.Notwithstanding the provisions of the preceding paragraph, exceptionally, and for justified reasons, minors under the age of 18 may be granted authorization to formalize the marriage provided that the female is at least 14 years of age and the male is 16 years of age.This authorization and exception can be granted by:1) the father and mother together, or one of them if the other has died or is deprived of parental authority;2) the adopter or adopters when the child has been adopted;3)  the guardian, if the minor is subject to guardianship;4) maternal or paternal grandparents, indistinctly, in the absence of the previous ones, preferring those wholive in the same household with the minor;5) only one of the entitled, when the other who must give it jointly with him is prevented from doing so;6) the court, if for reasons contrary to the principles and norms of socialist society, the persons empowered to do so refuse to grant the authorization.

Result: Yes, without discrimination based on sex/gender
Analysis [EN]: The Constitution of Fiji enshrines the right to education for all without discrimination on the ground of sex.Constitution of the Republic of Fiji of 2013 Article 26. (1). Every person is equal before the law and has the right to equal protection, treatment and benefit of the law.(2). Equality includes the full and equal enjoyment of all rights and freedoms recognised in this Chapter or any other written law.(3). A person must not be unfairly discriminated against, directly or indirectly on the grounds of his or her— (a) actual or supposed personal characteristics or circumstances, including race, culture, ethnic or social origin, colour, place of origin, sex, gender, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, birth, primary language, economic or social or health status, disability, age, religion, conscience, marital status or pregnancy; or (b) opinions or beliefs, except to the extent that those opinions or beliefs involve harm to others or the diminution of the rights or freedoms of others, or on any other ground prohibited by this Constitution.Article 31(1). Indicators: Are 9 years of primary and secondary education legally compulsory?
Analysis [EN]: The Framework Law on Education of 2010 guarantees compulsory basic education, which corresponds to primary and lower secondary education according to ISCED, for a duration of 9 years, from the age of six years old. The Framework Law on Education of 2010 (unofficial translation)Article 12. (1). Basic education is universal and compulsory.Article 13. (1). Basic education takes place during 9 years of schooling and is organized in three cycles:1. The first cycle goes from the 1st to the 4th grade of schooling, being subdivided in two phases, organized the following way: (a) First phase, which includes 1st and 2nd grade of schooling; (b) Second phase, which includes 3rd and 4th grade of schooling. 2. The second cycle, that shapes the third phase of basic education, includes the 5th and 6th grade; 3. The third cycle, that comprises the 7th, 8th and 9th grade of schooling, constitutes the fourth and last phase of basic education. (4) Are admitted to basic education the children who complete 6 years old until the 1st of October.

Indicators: General comments
Analysis [EN]: The Federal Republic of Nigeria has 36 states and a Federal Capital Territory located in Abuja. Its legal system is a mix of states’ legislation, customary law, Islamic law and English common law [1]. Each state has an independent legislature. A federal law may not adopted by all the states, such as the Child Rights Act of 2003, which is yet to be passed by 12 northern states.  Regarding education, it is regulated at the federal, state and local levels. The Compulsory, Free Universal Basic Education Act of 2004 is a law adopted at the federal level and setting minimum standards in education. Federal legal systems will be scored against the lowest-performing province, state or territory within that country. Therefore, for some indicators, the review of girls and womens right to education in Nigeria requires monitoring the states and local laws, to which UNESCO has not been able to access all.------[1] See Ngozi Efobi and Naomi Ekop, ǼLEX, “Legal systems in Nigeria: Overview”, available on Thomson Reuters Practical Law (accessed on 08/2021).

Indicators: Does the Constitution enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Result: Yes, without discrimination based on sex/gender
Analysis [EN]: The Constitution of Serbia enshrines the right to education and contains a provision on equality and non-discrimination on the ground of sex.Constitution of the Republic of Serbia of 2006 (unofficial translation) Article 21. All are equal before the Constitution and law. Everyone shall have the right to equal legal protection, without discrimination. All direct or indirect discrimination based on any grounds, particularly on race, sex, national origin, social origin, birth, religion, political or other opinion, property status, culture, language, age, mental or physical disability shall be prohibited.Article 71. Everyone shall have the right to education. Primary education is mandatory and free, whereas secondary education is free. All citizens shall have access under equal conditions to higher education. The Republic of Serbia shall provide for free tertiary education to successful and talented students of lower property status in accordance with the law. Establishment of schools and universities shall be regulated by the law.

Indicators: Are learners legally protected against all violence and corporal punishment in educational institutions?
Analysis [EN]: The Law on Prohibition of Discrimination does not explicitly apply to educational settings but the Law on the Foundations of the Education System does guarantee protection against all forms of violence and corporal punishment. Law on Prohibition of Discrimination of 2009 (unofficial translation)Article 20. … Physical and other violence, exploitation, hatred, belittling, blackmailing and harassment based on gender are prohibited, as well as advocating, supporting and acting on prejudices, customs and other social behaviors based on the idea of ​​subordination of stereotypical gender roles. Law on the Foundations of the Education System of 2017 (unofficial translation)Article 111. The institution prohibits physical, psychological, social, sexual, digital and any other violence, abuse and neglect of an employee, child, student, adult, parent or other legal representative or third party in the institution.Violations of the prohibition referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article, which an employee commits against another employee of the institution, shall be regulated by law.Violence and abuse mean any form of one-off or repeated verbal or non-verbal behavior that results in a real or potential threat to the health, development and dignity of the personality of a child, a student and an adult.Neglect and negligence is a failure of the institution or employee to provide the conditions for the proper development of the child, the student and the adult.The institution is obliged to report immediately to the competent authority if there is evidence of violence, abuse or neglect in the child, student or adult.Physical violence, within the meaning of this Law, means: the physical punishment of a child, a student or an adult by an employee, a parent or other legal representative or a third party in an institution; any conduct that may result in actual or potential bodily harm to a child, student, adult or employee; violent behavior of the employee towards the child, student or adult, as well as the student and adult towards another student, adult or employee.Psychic violence, within the meaning of this Law, is considered to be conduct that leads to an immediate or permanent threat to mental and emotional health and dignity.Social violence, within the meaning of this law, is considered to involve a child, a student and an adult from a group of peers and various forms of activity of the institution.Sexual violence and abuse, within the meaning of this Law, means conduct that sexually harasses, alleges, or coerces a child and student into engaging in sexual activities that he or she does not want, understand, or for which he or she has not developed or used for prostitution, pornography, and other forms of sexual exploitation.Digital violence and abuse, within the meaning of this Law, are considered misuse of information and communication technologies that may result in personal injury and harm to their dignity and are effected by sending e-mail, sms, mms, via website ( web site), by reading, engaging in forums, social networks and other forms of digital communication.The institution is obliged to report to the competent authority any form of violence, abuse and neglect in the institution committed by the parents, that is, another legal representative or a third party in the institution.

Indicators: Does the Constitution enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Analysis [EN]: The Constitution of the Seychelles enshrines the right to education for every citizen but it does not apply to all within the territory. It contains a general but limited non-discrimination provision, which does not include sex or gender as a prohibited ground.Constitution of Seychelles of 1993, as amended in 2011Article 27(1). Every person has a right to equal protection of the law including the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms set out in this Charter without discrimination on any ground except as is necessary in a democratic society.Article 33. The State recognises the right of every citizen to education and with a view to ensuring the effective realization of this right undertakes− (a). to provide compulsory education, which shall be free in State schools, for such minimum period, which shall not be less than ten years, as may be prescribed by law; (b). to ensure that the educational programmes in all schools are aimed at the complete development of the person; (c). to afford, on the basis of intellectual capability, every citizen equal access to educational opportunities and facilities beyond the period of compulsory education; (d). to allow, subject to such reasonable restrictions, supervision and conditions as are necessary in a democratic society, any person, organization or institution to establish and maintain a private school;(e). to respect the right of parents to choose whether to send their children to a State or private school

Indicators: Does the Constitution enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Analysis [EN]: The Constitution of Sierra Leone does not comprehensively enshrine the right to education as it only states that the government shall direct is policy towards ensuring that there are equal rights and adequate educational opportunities for all citizens at all levels. There is a general provision which provides that the State shall discourage discrimination based on several grounds, including sex. Constitution of Sierra Leone of 1991Article 6. Indicators: Is the legal age of marriage set at least at 18 years old?
Analysis [EN]: Under the Child Rights Act of 2007, the minimum legal age of marriage is 18 years. However, this is contradicted by the Customary Marriage and Divorce Act 2009 which permits marriages below 18 years of age with parental or judicial consent and which does not gives an absolute minimum age.Civil Marriage Act of 1960 [1]Article 7. …the Registrar… shall not issue such certificate until one of the two parties to the intended marriage shall appear personally and make an affidavit … (b) that each of the parties to the intended marriage (not being a widower or widow) is – (c) In the case of a person whose personal law is customary law not less than eighteen years of age; and (ii) in every other case not less than twenty-one year of age, and where one of the parties is under the age of eighteen or twenty-one as the case may be, that the consent of the person or persons whose consent to such marriage is required by law has been obtained.d) If the personal law of the either of the parties to the proposed marriage is customary law, that the following conditions have been fulfilled- (i) That neither of the parties is a party to the subsisting marriage; (ii) if the woman is under 18 years of age, that at least one of her parents or guardians has given his or her consent.Child Rights Act of 2007Article 2. In this Act, … “child” means a person below the age of eighteenArticle 34.(1) The minimum age of marriage of whatever kind shall be eighteen years.(2) No person shall force a child … (c) to be married.(3) Notwithstanding any law to the contrary, no certificate, licence or registration shall be granted in respect of any marriage unless the registrar or other responsible officer is satisfied that the parties to the marriage are of the age of maturityThe Registration of Customary Marriage and Divorce Act of 2009 [2]Article 2.(1) Subject to this Act, a customary marriage, contracted after the coming into operation of this Act, shall be valid only if –(a) both spouses are not less than eighteen years old and consent to the marriage…(2) Where, either of the prospective spouses, not being a widow or widower, is less than eighteen years, it shall be necessary for the parents to give consent to the marriage and if the parents are dead or unable for any reason to give such consent, then the consent may be given by the guardians of the prospective spouse or spouses to the marriage, as the case may be.(3) If the consent of the parents or guardians cannot be obtained or is unreasonably withheld, a Magistrate or Local Government Chief Administrator of the locality in which the marriage is to take place may give his consent. ------------------[1] Retrieved from https://landwise.resourceequity.org/documents/1304[2] Retrieved from http://www.sierra-leone.org/Laws/2009-01.pdf

Indicators: Is pregnant and parenting girls’ right to education protected in the legal framework?
Analysis [EN]: While no disposition prohibiting pregnant and parenting girls to attend school has been identified in the legislation, it has been documented that, following a statement from the Ministry of Education, pregnant girls were prohibited to go to mainstream school. Analysis [EN]: While no explicit protection against violence existed in the previous act, the new Education Act of 2023 explicitly prohibits corporal punishment, other forms of degrading punishments as well as all other forms of violence, including psychological, physical and sexual violence. (1) A learning environment shall be conducive; physically and psychologically safe, free from all forms of violence and abuse and facilitates learning.(3) A member of the staff of a school or person engaged to teach or support teaching at a school, shall not bully; harass, verbally abuse, physically abuse, sexually abuse or exploit children in his care(4) Cyber bullying by a teacher or school authority against a pupil is prohibited.Article 72. (1) Corporal punishment and all other forms of degrading punishment designed to cause, or create fear of physical pain in a pupil, administered or threatened for the purposes of domination or control are prohibited.Article 72. (2) A member of staff of a school, or a person engaged to teach or support teaching at a school, shall not administer corporal punishment to a pupil of that school.Article 72. (3) A person, including a relative of a pupil, shall not(a) administer corporal punishment to a pupil on school grounds; or(b) threaten a pupil with corporal punishment on the school grounds. …Article 72. (4) Alternative forms of discipline including positive methods may be employed for child development.Article 73. (1) Bullying, harassment, verbal abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse and exploitation of a pupil by another pupil is prohibited.Prevention of Cruelty to Children Act 1926Article 3. Nothing in this Ordinance shall be construed to take away or affect the right of any parent, teacher or other person having the lawful control or charge of a child to administer punishment to such child.

Indicators: Does the Constitution enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Result: Yes, without discrimination based on sex/gender
Analysis [EN]: The Constitution of Zimbabwe enshrines the right to education but only for citizens and permanent residents. It creates an obligation for the State to take measures to ensure that girls are afforded the same educational opportunities as boys and contains a principle of non-discrimination based on sex and gender and an equality principle for men and women. Constitution of Zimbabwe of 2013 as amended in 2021  Article 27(2). The State must take measures to ensure that girls are afforded the same opportunities as boys to obtain education at all levels. Article 56. Equality and non-discrimination (1) All persons are equal before the law and have the right to equal protection and benefit of the law. (2) Women and men have the right to equal treatment, including the right to equal opportunities in political, economic, cultural and social spheres. (3) Every person has the right not to be treated in an unfairly discriminatory manner on such grounds as their nationality, race, colour, tribe, place of birth, ethnic or social origin, language, class, religious belief, political affiliation, opinion, custom, culture, sex, gender, marital status, age, pregnancy, disability or economic or social status, or whether they were born in or out of wedlock. Article 75. Right to Education(1) Every citizen and permanent resident of Zimbabwe has a right to— (a) a basic State-funded education, including adult basic education; and (b) further education, which the State, through reasonable legislative and other measures, must make progressively available and accessible ... (4) The State must take reasonable legislative and other measures, within the limits of the resources available to it, to achieve the progressive realisation of the right set out in subsection (1).

Indicators: Does the legislation enshrine the right to education without discrimination?
Analysis [EN]: The legislation of Zimbabwe does not fully enshrine the right to education as it is limited to children. It contains an equality of rights provision without distinction based on, among other, gender and sex.Education Act [Chapter 25:04] of 1987, as amended in 2020 Section 4. Children’s fundamental right to education in Zimbabwe (1) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other enactment, but subject to this Act, every child in Zimbabwe shall have the right to school education. (1a) The State shall ensure the provision of sanitary ware and other menstrual health facilities to girls in all schools to promote menstrual health.(2) Subject to subsection (5), no child in Zimbabwe shall— (a) be refused admission to any school; or (b) be discriminated against by the imposition of onerous terms and conditions in regard to his or her admission to, suspended, excluded or expelled from any school on the grounds of his or her nationality, race, colour, tribe, place of birth, ethnic or social origin, language, class religious belief, political affiliation, opinion, custom, culture, sex, gender, marital status, age, pregnancy, disability or economic or social status, or whether they were born in or out of wedlock.

Indicators: Are 12 years of primary and secondary education legally free?
Analysis [EN]: The legislation does not guarantee free education. According to the Education Act, pupils shall not be required to pay fees or levies for basic state funded education. However, the same Act also prescribes for fees which shall be payable for instruction in government schools and that the objective is to provide this tuition fees for the lowest possible fee.Education Act [Chapter 25:04] of 1987, as amended in 2020 Section 2. Interpretation… “basic state funded education” means(a) education from early childhood education up to form four; or(b) adult education up to form four; or(c) any other category as may be declared as such by the Minister by notice in the Gazette from time to time: for which pupils shall not be required to pay fees or levies and the State shall provide them with learning and teaching material, facilities, infrastructure and resources subject to the provisions of section 75 of the Constitution …Section 5. Compulsory education(1) Every child shall be entitled to compulsory basic state funded education.Section 6. Minimum fees for education. Indicators: Are learners legally protected against all violence and corporal punishment in educational institutions?
Analysis [EN]: The 2020 amendment of the Education Act provides protection from corporal punishment in schools. However, the 2014 Criminal law has not yet been amended to reflect the recent amendment of the Education Act and therefore still prescribes that school-teachers have authority to administer moderate corporal punishment for disciplinary purposes upon minor male pupils or students, whilst corporal punishment upon a female pupil or student is prohibited. Therefore, this lack of harmonization is reflected in the score. No other legal dispositions regarding violence in schools have been identified.Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act [Chapter 9:23] as amended in 2019Section 241. Discipline of children(2) Subject to this section, …(b) a school-teacher shall have authority to administer moderate corporal punishment for disciplinary purposes upon any minor male pupil or student(4) No school-teacher or person acting under authority delegated to him or her by a school-teacher shall administer corporal punishment upon a female pupil or student.(5) When administering corporal punishment upon a minor male pupil or student at his or her school, a school-teacher shall comply with any lawful rules, regulations or administrative instructions which apply to the administration of corporal punishment at his or her schoolEducation Act [Chapter 25:04] of 1987, as amended in 2020Section 68A. Pupil discipline(1) The responsible authority of every school shall draw up a disciplinary policy for the school in accordance with standards set out in regulations prescribed by the Minister for the purpose.(2) The regulations and any disciplinary policy shall—(a)not permit any treatment which—(i)does not respect the human dignity of a pupil; or(ii)amounts to physical or psychological torture, or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment; (b)prescribe the manner in which any punishment may be administered.(3) Disciplinary measures must be moderate, reasonable and proportionate in the light of the conduct, age, sex, health and circumstances of the pupil concerned and the best interests of the child shall be paramount …(5) Under no circumstance is a teacher allowed to beat a child.
